nameStory: The "adder's-mouth" name comes from the flower's shape, which resembles a snake's open mouth with its three-lobed lip (labellum) that looks like a forked tongue. The "green" part is straightforward - unlike its white-flowered cousin, this orchid's tiny blooms are distinctly green in color.
description: Green adder's-mouth is a small, secretive orchid that's easy to overlook in New England's forests. This delicate plant grows no taller than 20 inches and typically has just one oval leaf partway up its slender stem. What makes it special is its cluster of tiny green flowers at the top - sometimes over 100 of them packed into what looks like a miniature green bottle brush. It's one of our more common native orchids, though you need sharp eyes to spot it.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny green flowers clustered in a dense spike that starts rounded like a green marble, then stretches into a narrow tower. Each flower is barely 1/8 inch across with a distinctive three-lobed lip and backward-curving petals.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Usually just one smooth, oval leaf that wraps partway around the stem about halfway up. The leaf feels thin and papery, with parallel veins running lengthwise like other orchid family members.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A single slender stem rises from the forest floor, rarely over 20 inches tall. The whole plant has a delicate, almost translucent quality that helps it blend into dappled forest light.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, pale green stem that's often slightly ridged or angled rather than perfectly round. It feels firm but flexible, like a green drinking straw.

habitat: Look for green adder's-mouth in moist, rich woodlands with acidic soil, often among mosses and ferns. It favors spots with filtered light under deciduous or mixed forests, particularly areas that stay consistently damp but not waterlogged. You'll often find it growing alongside other woodland wildflowers like wild ginger and trout lily.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring, with the single leaf unfurling as the stem elongates. This is when the plant is easiest to spot before surrounding vegetation gets thick.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time in New England, with the dense cluster of green flowers fully developed. The flowers are most visible from late June through July when they're fresh and upright.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the plant begins to die back, though seed capsules may persist for a while. The leaf yellows and withers as the plant prepares for dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible. The underground bulb-like structure rests in the soil until next spring's emergence.

funFact: A single green adder's-mouth plant can produce up to 160 individual flowers on one tiny spike - that's more flowers than most showy garden plants, yet each bloom is so small you need a magnifying glass to see the intricate orchid structure!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young grass shoots or sedges before flowering, but the single oval leaf partway up the stem is the giveaway - grasses have narrow leaves from the base. Once flowering, the dense green flower spike is distinctive among New England orchids.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an "orchid," many people expect showy, colorful flowers like tropical orchids. Green adder's-mouth represents the subtle beauty of native orchids - they've evolved to blend in rather than stand out, relying on small pollinators rather than flashy displays.
compareHints: Green adder's-mouth differs from white adder's-mouth by its green (rather than white) flowers and typically taller growth. Unlike Appalachian adder's-mouth, which is extremely rare, green adder's-mouth usually has just one leaf rather than two, and its flowers are arranged in a denser, more compact cluster that elongates as it matures.

relatedSpecies.distinction: White adder's-mouth differs from green adder's-mouth by its paler, greenish-white flowers and single leaf that wraps around the stem base, while green adder's-mouth has distinctly green flowers and a single leaf that doesn't wrap the stem.
Unlike green adder's-mouth which has a single leaf at the base of the plant, Appalachian adder's-mouth has its leaf positioned higher up on the stem.
